definitions.definition: The yoga of force: the physical methods — postures, retentions, mudrās and bandhas, cleansing acts — that force the breath into the central channel and awaken kuṇḍalinī; taught 'solely for the sake of rājayoga' (HYP 1.2) and inseparable from it (HYP 2.76). The Yogabīja and the Jyotsnā gloss ha as the sun and ṭha as the moon, haṭha being their union, i.e. of prāṇa and apāna. The Śārṅgadhara Paddhati distinguishes Gorakṣa's haṭha from that of Mṛkaṇḍu's son.

The goal served by haṭha: samādhi, the mindless, supportless state in which mind and breath are dissolved; HYP 4.3–4 lists it first among the synonyms of samādhi (with unmanī, manonmanī, amanaska, sahaja, turyā…). The DYŚ calls it the best of the four yogas, the Śiva Saṃhitā 'free of duality'; the Jyotsnā identifies it with asamprajñāta yoga, the cessation of all mental activity.

equivalents.standpoint: the haṭha texts' list of synonyms
equivalents.note: HYP 4.3–4 and GS 7.17 treat rājayoga and samādhi as names of one state

definitions.definition: The yoga in which the mind is dissolved (cittalaya) through 'indications' (saṅketa) — fixing attention on the void, the nose-tip, the brow-centre, the back of the head, the big toes, lying like a corpse — of which Ādinātha taught eight crore (DYŚ 14–24); the third of the four yogas, given to the middling aspirant (SS 5.12). The HYP holds nādānusandhāna the chief laya.
The first and lowest of the four yogas: placing the mātṛkā letters on the body and repeating a mantra; fit for the mild (mṛdu) practitioner, who succeeds in twelve years (DYŚ 11–13; SS 5.11).
Yoga as one, though called fourfold (mantra, laya, haṭha, rāja) — a doctrine of the Yogabīja and the Haṭharatnāvalī (recalled).
The Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā's name for its yoga: the body (ghaṭa, 'pot') is baked in the fire of yoga through seven means (GS 1.1–11).

The channels of the subtle body carrying the breath: seventy-two thousand arise from the bulb (GŚ 16; HYP 1.39, 4.18), of which ten (or fourteen, SS 2.13, which counts 350,000 in all) are principal and three chief — iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā. When clogged with impurities the breath cannot enter the middle (HYP 2.4).

cross_language.note: the channel in Vajrayāna subtle-body teaching

definitions.definition: The cleansing of the channels, prerequisite to breath-control (HYP 2.4–10; GS 5.35–36: with seed-mantra, samanu, or by the cleansing acts, nirmanu); its signs are slimness, radiance, kindled fire, holding the breath at will and manifestation of nāda (HYP 2.19–20).
The left channel, of the moon, identified with the Gaṅgā (HYP 3.110); inhalation 'through the moon' begins alternate-nostril purification (HYP 2.7).
The right channel, of the sun, identified with the Yamunā (HYP 3.110).

The central channel through which prāṇa and awakened kuṇḍalinī rise; its synonyms are śūnyapadavī, brahmarandhra, mahāpatha, śmaśāna, śāmbhavī and madhyamārga (HYP 3.4); of the 72,000 channels it alone is the śāmbhavī śakti (4.18); it 'devours time' (4.17).

equivalents.note: HYP 3.4 lists brahmarandhra among the synonyms of suṣumnā; elsewhere (SS 2.18, 5.123–130) the brahmarandhra is an aperture within or at the end of suṣumnā

definitions.definition: A subtle channel within suṣumnā (within vajrā, per the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa), 'dear to Śiva', in which is the brahmarandhra (SS 2.18).
The channel within suṣumnā, enclosing citriṇī (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa).
The innermost path by which breath and kuṇḍalinī rise (HYP 2.46, 3.69); in the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa the channel within citriṇī.
A name of suṣumnā (HYP 3.4) and the subtle opening within it; kuṇḍalinī sleeps at its mouth (SS 4.14); fixing the mind there frees from sin (SS 5.141, recalled).
The egg-shaped bulb between the genitals and navel from which the channels arise (GŚ 16); kuṇḍalinī sleeps above it (HYP 3.107).

The power (śakti) coiled at the base of the central channel, blocking its mouth; the support of all yoga (HYP 3.1); awakened by the guru's grace (3.2) and by breath, locks and mudrās (3.5, 3.66–69), she pierces the lotuses and knots and makes the mind supportless. Synonyms: kuṭilāṅgī, bhujaṅgī, śakti, īśvarī, kuṇḍalī, arundhatī (3.104); coiled eightfold (GŚ 30) or three and a half times (ṢCN). For yogins she is for liberation, for fools for bondage (HYP 3.107).

equivalents.note: the Vajrayāna inner fire (caṇḍālī, gtum mo) that rises in the central channel; functional analogy only — the traditions do not identify them

definitions.definition: A name of kuṇḍalinī (HYP 3.104; 'the sleeping Arundhatī', 3.119).
Kuṇḍalinī as the young ascetic widow seated between the Gaṅgā (iḍā) and Yamunā (piṅgalā), to be seized by force (HYP 3.109–110).
The three knots — of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra — pierced in succession by the awakened power; in the HYP their piercing marks the first, second and fourth stages of nāda (4.70–77).
The first knot; when pierced in the beginning stage, bliss from the void and tinkling inner sounds arise (HYP 4.70).
The second knot, pierced in the ghaṭa stage, when a kettledrum sound is heard in the extreme void (HYP 4.73).
The third knot, pierced in niṣpatti, when the breath reaches Śiva's seat and flute and vīṇā sounds arise (HYP 4.76).

A centre of the subtle body along the central channel; the texts differ in number and attributes — six plus the thousand-petalled lotus (ṢCN; GŚ), nine (Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati), with sixteen supports (ādhāra), three targets and five voids in the Nāth body-maps.

cross_language.note: the Vajrayāna channel-wheels (usually four or five)

definitions.definition: (1) The root centre (GŚ 10). (2) The sixteen supports of the body on which breath and attention are fixed; jālandhara 'binds the sixteen ādhāras' (HYP 3.73); the Haṭhatattvakaumudī devotes a chapter to them.
An object of fixed attention; the Nāth body-map counts three (inner, outer, middle); śāmbhavī mudrā is attention on an inner target with the gaze outward (HYP 4.36).
Space as a place of the subtle body: the 'space-wheel' (vyomacakra) of khecarī between sun and moon (HYP 3.37, 4.45); the five voids (vyomapañcaka) of the Nāth body-map.
The first centre at the perineum/anus, four-petalled, of earth (LAṂ), seat of sleeping kuṇḍalinī and of the triangular yoni with the self-born liṅga (GŚ 10–12; ṢCN 4–13).
The second centre at the genitals, six-petalled, of water (VAṂ); GŚ 14 derives the name from 'sva' = prāṇa.
The navel centre, ten-petalled, of fire (RAṂ), where the bulb is strung on suṣumnā like a jewel (GŚ 15).
The heart centre, twelve-petalled, of air (YAṂ), where the unstruck sound is heard (ṢCN; GŚ 60).
The throat centre, sixteen-petalled, of space (HAṂ) (ṢCN).
The two-petalled centre between the brows, of mind, with the praṇava (ṢCN); HYP 4.48 calls the place between the brows the place of Śiva.
The thousand-petalled lotus at or above the crown, seat of Śiva (Kailāsa, SS 5.151–157; Paramaśiva, ṢCN 40–49), where kuṇḍalinī dissolves and nectar flows.
The breath as wind: ten vāyus move in the channels as the living soul's vehicles (GŚ 23–25; SS 3.4–8); when the wind moves the mind moves (HYP 2.2).

The breath: life is its staying in the body and death its departure (HYP 2.3); as one of the ten vāyus it abides in the heart (SS 3.7); with apāna it pulls the living soul up and down (GŚ 26–29); their union is the aim of mūlabandha (HYP 3.64).
The downward breath at the anus (SS 3.7); turned upward by mūlabandha it meets fire and prāṇa and awakens kuṇḍalinī (HYP 3.61–69).
The breath at the navel (SS 3.7).
The breath in the throat (SS 3.7).
The breath pervading the whole body (SS 3.7).
Minor breath causing belching (SS 3.8, one of the five beginning with nāga).
Minor breath causing the opening (and closing) of the eyes (SS 3.8).
Minor breath causing hunger (SS 3.8; attributions vary between texts).
Minor breath causing yawning (SS 3.8).
Minor breath associated with hiccup in SS 3.8; other texts say it pervades the body and remains after death (recalled).

Breath-control, practised after posture is firm (HYP 2.1); threefold as exhalation, inhalation and retention (2.71); correct practice destroys disease, improper practice causes it (2.16–17); the Jyotsnā identifies haṭha itself with prāṇāyāma, the union of prāṇa and apāna.

Breath-retention: of two kinds, sahita (with inhalation and exhalation) and kevala (alone) (HYP 2.71); eight named varieties in HYP 2.44 and a different eight in GS 5.47. Extreme retention is restricted in this ontology (summary only).
Spontaneous retention free of inhalation and exhalation; when mastered nothing is unattainable and rājayoga is reached (HYP 2.73–75); no retention equals it (1.43).
Exhalation, one of the three parts of breath-control (HYP 2.71).
Inhalation (HYP 2.71).

A lock that contains the breath: mūla (root), uḍḍiyāna (abdominal) and jālandhara (throat), together the 'three locks' practised by the great Siddhas (HYP 3.74–76); applied at the end of inhalation and of retention (2.45–46).

In haṭha, a bodily technique that seals and redirects breath, bindu and kuṇḍalinī — ten in the HYP (3.6–7), twenty-five in the GS (3.1–3); to be kept secret and learned from a guru (HYP 3.8–9, 3.129).
A (divine) technique — used of the mudrās (HYP 1.56, 1.67) and especially of viparītakaraṇī, which cheats the sun of the nectar (3.78).

The six cleansing acts — dhauti, basti, neti, trāṭaka, nauli, kapālabhāti (HYP 2.22) — needed only by those with excess fat or phlegm (2.21); some teachers hold breath-control alone suffices (2.37); the GS gives them to all as the first means (1.12); later texts count eight.

Moderate diet: smooth, sweet food eaten to please Śiva, leaving a quarter of the stomach empty (HYP 1.58); chief of the yamas (HYP 1.38; DYŚ 30); without it yoga brings disease (GS 5.16); half food, a quarter water, a quarter air (GS 5.22).
The yogin's small secluded hut, whose place and construction the HYP (1.12–13) and GS (5.5–7) prescribe.
The status of haṭha teachings: 'kept secret it is potent, revealed it is impotent' (HYP 1.11); mudrās to be guarded like a jewel box (3.9).

Fitness for a practice: the Śiva Saṃhitā assigns the four yogas to four grades of aspirant (5.10–14); the Jyotsnā holds the dispassionate alone properly eligible though Purāṇic verses grant yoga to all beings; the HYP and DYŚ say anyone who practises succeeds.

The state in which the mind is transcended; it cannot arise while the channels are impure (HYP 2.4); a synonym of samādhi (4.3); through it duality is not perceived (4.61) and the body becomes like a log (4.106).
The steadiness of mind when the breath moves in the middle (HYP 2.42); the one state (3.54); saluted as a goddess (4.64).
The mindless state, a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4); the name and goal of the Amanaska's rājayoga, attained effortlessly by the guru's grace (Amanaska 2).

As salt dissolves in water, the union of self and mind; the sameness when breath is exhausted and mind dissolved; the union of individual and supreme self with all intention ceased (HYP 4.5–7); sixfold in the GS (7.5–6).
The sameness that arises when breath is exhausted and mind dissolved (HYP 4.6; GŚ 94).

The natural state (sahajāvasthā), a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4), which arises of itself when śakti is awakened (4.11) but is hard to obtain without a true guru's compassion (4.9); 'natural bliss' in the paricaya stage (4.75).

The void: a name of suṣumnā's path (śūnyapadavī, HYP 3.3–4); the breath dissolves in the void (4.10); the nāda stages pass through śūnya, atiśūnya and mahāśūnya (4.70–75); 'empty within, empty without' (4.56).
The fourth state, a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4); the place between the brows where mind dissolves and time does not exist (4.48).
The stainless state reached by devotion to Śiva the guru (HYP 4.1), a synonym of samādhi (4.4), in which mind and breath dissolve (4.105).
Without support: the mind made supportless at the end of retention (HYP 2.77) or when kuṇḍalinī wakes (3.3); 'one god is the supportless' (3.54); a synonym of samādhi (4.4).
Immortality, a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.3), and the conquest of death sought through retaining bindu and nectar.
What remains when the mind is dissolved by abandoning the knowable (HYP 4.62).
A synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4); the yogin in samādhi is 'liberated' though living (4.107–112); from nirguṇa meditation and samādhi one becomes jīvanmukta (DYŚ 114).
In the HYP the state to be practised for through khecarī: for one who attains yogic sleep 'there is never time' (4.49).

Dissolution of mind (with breath): 'the forgetting of objects because latent impressions do not arise again' (HYP 4.34); the lord of the breath, resting on nāda (4.29); Ādinātha taught a crore and a quarter kinds, of which nāda is chief (4.66).

The inner sound heard in the purified suṣumnā; laya rests on it (HYP 4.29); its stages and sounds mark the four stages of yoga (4.69–77, 4.84–86); whatever is heard as nāda is śakti, the soundless is the supreme Brahman (4.101–102).
The sound not produced by striking, heard within when the knot of Brahmā is pierced (HYP 4.70); within its resonance is the knowable and within that the mind, which dissolves there (4.100).
Success in yoga, and the powers that arise (distant hearing and seeing, speed, invisibility, turning metal to gold, flight — DYŚ 89–90) which the yogin must regard as obstacles and hide (DYŚ 91–94).
The first of the four stages: brahmagranthi pierced, tinkling sounds, a radiant, fragrant, healthy body (HYP 4.70–71; SS 3.29–31).
(1) The body as a pot (GS 1.6–8; HYP 2.23). (2) The second stage, when the breath 'made one' enters the middle and prāṇa–apāna, mind–breath, individual and supreme self unite (HYP 4.72; DYŚ 81–83).
The third stage: the breath reaches the great void; drum sound; natural bliss (HYP 4.74–75); the breath enters suṣumnā and pierces the centres (DYŚ 97–99; SS 3.60–61).
The fourth stage: rudragranthi pierced, flute and vīṇā sounds, the mind one — rājayoga (HYP 4.76–77); it gives both enjoyment and liberation (DYŚ 147).
Posture, the first limb of haṭha, giving steadiness, health and lightness (HYP 1.17); Śiva taught 84 (HYP 1.33) or 8,400,000 (GS 2.1).

Withdrawal: bringing the wandering mind back under the self's control (GS 4.1–2); withdrawing the senses while in retention and seeing all as the self (DYŚ 84–88); the sun's 'drawing in' of the moon's nectar (GŚ 55); moving breath through the eighteen marmas (YY, VS).
Concentration, especially the five element-concentrations holding breath and mind in the regions of earth, water, fire, air and space (DYŚ 100–110; GŚ 68–75).
Meditation: with and without qualities (GŚ 76–77; DYŚ 111–114); gross, of light and subtle (GS 6.1).

The sun in the body: the fire at the navel (GŚ 57) and the right channel; it swallows the nectar that drips from the moon, and so the body ages (HYP 3.77); sun and moon make time, suṣumnā devours it (4.17).
The moon in the head / at the root of the palate, made of nectar, raining downward (GŚ 57–58; SS 2.6–9); the left channel; in the Amṛtasiddhi identified with bindu.

The nectar of immortality dripping from the moon in the head, lost to the sun's fire unless saved by viparītakaraṇī, jālandhara and khecarī (HYP 3.72, 3.77–79; DYŚ 127–128); drinking it the yogin conquers death.
In the haṭha texts the moon's nectar: 'drinking soma' with the tongue turned up (HYP 3.44); the body filled with the moon's digit (somakalā) is not abandoned by the soul (HYP 3.45–46; GŚ 66).

The vital essence (semen; with rajas in women), identified with the moon (Amṛtasiddhi); 'death by the fall of bindu, life by holding bindu' (HYP 3.88); its control is a sign of success (2.78); mind, breath and bindu are made steady together (4.28). Cosmologically bindu is Śiva and rajas Śakti (SS 1.92); Śiva's nature is nāda, bindu and kalā (HYP 4.1).

cross_language.note: the drops of the Vajrayāna subtle body

equivalents.note: the white bodhicitta/drop of Buddhist tantra in the Amṛtasiddhi's milieu; functional analogy, not an identity asserted by either tradition

definitions.definition: The female generative fluid, counterpart of bindu, retained by the yoginī in the vajrolī passage (HYP 3.99–102) and identified with Śakti (SS 1.92). Not the guṇa rajas.

(1) The mudrā in which the tongue, reversed, enters the cavity above the palate and the gaze is between the brows — best of mudrās (HYP 1.43, 3.32); RESTRICTED. (2) In HYP 4.43–47, the state in which the breath moves in the middle between sun and moon; the name is explained as 'the mind moves in space (kha) and the tongue moves in space' (3.41).
A mudrā for retaining and drawing up bindu (and rajas), with the variants sahajolī and amarolī (HYP 3.83–103; DYŚ 137–143). RESTRICTED: summary only.
A variant of vajrolī reported by the HYP as practised by the Kāpālikas of the Khaṇḍa school (3.96). RESTRICTED: summary only.
A variant of vajrolī involving ash; said to succeed only for the virtuous and envy-free (HYP 3.92–95). RESTRICTED: summary only.
The throat lock that binds the network of channels and stops the nectar falling into the fire (HYP 3.70–73; DYŚ 126–128).
The abdominal lock by which prāṇa 'flies up' suṣumnā; best of the locks, giving liberation naturally when firm (HYP 3.55–60).
Contracting the root so that apāna rises; by it prāṇa and apāna, nāda and bindu become one (HYP 3.61–65).
The practice that puts the sun above and moon below so the nectar is not swallowed by the sun, learned only from the guru's mouth (HYP 3.77–82; GŚ 59).
Attention fixed on an inner target with the gaze outward and unblinking, kept secret like a woman of good family (HYP 4.35–37); also a name of suṣumnā (3.4; 4.18).
The mudrā that stirs and raises kuṇḍalinī (HYP 3.104–123). RESTRICTED as an advanced energy practice.
The confluence of the three channels (iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā — Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī), which mahābandha brings about (HYP 3.24).
The sixth kind of samādhi in the GS (7.6, 7.16), and in the HYP the effect of mūrcchā retention (2.69).
In HYP 3.47–48, 'eating cow's flesh' means the entry of the tongue (go) into the palate in khecarī — a transgressive expression given a yogic sense.
The essence flowing from the moon when the tongue enters the palate, called 'liquor' in HYP 3.47–49.
Mercury, which like the mind is by nature unsteady; 'bound' mercury and mind are compared in HYP 4.26–27 (an alchemical analogy; no procedure).
One of the two causes of mind (with breath): if either is destroyed both are (HYP 4.22); laya is forgetting objects when vāsanās no longer arise (4.34).
What saves (carries across), which those confused by Āgamas, Vedas and logic do not know (HYP 4.40); in the Yoga Upaniṣads a form of rājayoga.
In the Dattātreyayogaśāstra, the 'indications' — points of fixed attention — by which the mind dissolves in layayoga; Ādinātha taught eight crore (DYŚ 14–24).

literal: sound, tone; (here) the flow of breath

definitions.definition: In the svara science, the flow of breath through the left, right or both nostrils and the elements arising in it (Śiva Svarodaya).
(1) Reality, to which the mind is joined and dissolves (HYP 4.59). (2) In the svara science, the five elements present in the flow of breath (Śiva Svarodaya).
The body as microcosm containing Meru, the continents, stars and gods (SS 2.1–5).
The cosmos, and the body so named because it contains the cosmos (SS 1.91, 2.6; the thousand-petalled lotus is outside the body called brahmāṇḍa, SS 5.151).
The body 'ripened' in the fire of yoga (liberated) versus the unripe body subject to karma and rebirth (Yogabīja).
What the yogin sees in the stage of paricaya: the 'three peaks' of his karma (SS 3.61).
The eighteen vital points of the body through which the breath is moved in one kind of withdrawal (Yoga Yājñavalkya; Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā).

The conquest or postponement of death through yoga: the Siddhas break the staff of time (HYP 1.9); mudrās give 'cheating of time' (3.130); one established in rājayoga cheats time (4.103); a chapter of the Haṭhatattvakaumudī is devoted to it.
The breath, which goes out thirty-six finger-breadths (GŚ 40); the haṃsa in the thousand-petalled lotus (GS 6.10; Pādukāpañcaka).
The perfected masters of haṭha — Ādinātha, Matsyendra, Gorakṣa and the others — who by haṭha broke the staff of time (HYP 1.5–9).
The first of the ten mudrās; kuṇḍalinī becomes straight like a snake struck with a stick (HYP 3.10–14); first taught in the Amṛtasiddhi. (Not the Buddhist Mahāmudrā realization.)
The second mudrā, which stops the upward movement of all channels except the central and brings about the triple confluence (HYP 3.19–24).
The third mudrā, without which mahāmudrā and mahābandha are fruitless (HYP 3.25–29).
Bodily perfection claimed as a fruit of vajrolī (HYP 3.103) and of the haṭha practices generally.
